1. Introduction

1.1. The way we vote in a polling station has changed little since the Ballot Act 1872. As society becomes increasingly digital and expectations for convenience rise, existing processes are often at odds with people’s expectations of modern public services and in conflict with how some Returning Officers want to provide access to elections.

1.2. In its manifesto, the government committed to encouraging greater participation in our democracy. Modernising the voting experience is key to achieving that goal. To support this, the government is exploring ways to make voting in person more efficient, more convenient, and better aligned with the expectations of today’s electors.

1.3. As part of this work, the government partnered with four local authorities to pilot a range of flexible voting options at the local elections in May 2026.

1.4. We are now inviting formal applications from local authorities in England to pilot at local elections in May 2027.

1.5. If you would like to apply to pilot, we are inviting formal applications by 15 September 2026. Details of how to make a formal application are set out in this prospectus. If you have any questions or would like a discussion on piloting prior to submitting a formal application, please get in touch.

For pilot scheme enquiries, email: electionspilots@communities.gov.uk.

2. Objectives

2026 pilots

2.1. The previous round of flexible voting pilots was delivered in partnership with four local authorities at the May 2026 local elections. Cambridge City Council, North Hertfordshire District Council and Tunbridge Wells Borough Council piloted early in-person voting at hubs, giving electors the option to vote in the days ahead of polling day, alongside normal polling station provision on polling day. Milton Keynes City Council piloted on-the-day voting in a central voting hub, testing the impact of providing a centrally located hub on polling day in addition to usual polling stations.

2.2. Operational delivery of the pilots was successful, with no significant issues observed, demonstrating the viability of the pilot models. The Electoral Commission has published its statutory evaluation of the 2026 pilots. The report found that the pilots operated successfully, that voters who used the flexible voting options were generally positive about their experience and that there is appetite for greater flexibility in how people vote. The Commission also concluded that further testing is needed to strengthen the evidence base. MHCLG is continuing its own evaluation of the 2026 pilots, and the findings from both evaluations will inform future policy development and piloting activity.

Participating in the early voting pilot was a genuinely rewarding experience and provided valuable insight into how greater flexibility can support voter engagement. It highlighted the importance of early planning, particularly around venues and suppliers, as well as the scale of communications needed to ensure electors understood the changes. While our approach worked well in Cambridge, it will be interesting to see how other areas tailor flexible voting to reflect their own local contexts and elector needs.

Vicky Jenner, Electoral Services Manager, Cambridge City Council

2027 objectives

2.3. The flexible voting pilot schemes are designed to explore innovative approaches to voting that better reflect the needs and expectations of today’s electorate. These pilots aim to modernise the voting experience by introducing greater flexibility, improving accessibility and enhancing voter satisfaction while safeguarding the integrity, security and transparency of the democratic process.

2.4. Following the pilots during the May 2026 local elections, we are aiming to test flexible voting in more places and further build the evidence base.

2.5. The Electoral Commission’s evaluation highlighted the need for additional evidence from a wider range of authorities and electoral contexts before firm conclusions can be reached about the impact of flexible voting. The 2027 pilots will provide an opportunity to expand the evidence base and test these approaches in different settings.

2.6. We are inviting local authorities to trial various piloting options as set out in section 3. There is also scope for local authorities to propose alternative options for pilots tailored to the needs of their electorate. However, we will not accept proposals for online or electronic voting.

2.7. The overarching objectives of these pilots are to:

improve voter convenience and satisfaction

advance accessibility and inclusive participation

assess feasibility and deliver cost-effective, resilient and secure voting

2.8. To improve voter convenience and satisfaction, the pilots will primarily test two options: voting hubs on polling day and early voting in hubs. These options are intended to make voting more accessible in terms of time and location, helping electors participate in a way that fits more easily into their lives. By offering greater choice and convenience, the pilots aim to support a more positive voting experience and encourage repeat engagement.

2.9. To advance accessibility and inclusive participation, the pilots will explore how flexible voting methods can better support electors who may face barriers to participation, such as disabled voters, those in remote areas, those with non-standard working patterns, and communities that are less likely to engage. Accessibility will be considered throughout the development and evaluation of pilot models.

8.3. This allows us to make a comprehensive, evidence-based assessment of the impact of implementing new practices and determine whether they are successful in delivering the desired outcomes. We can then make an informed decision about which measures should be implemented.

8.4. Previous pilots have tested a range of new and innovative solutions and have informed policy making in both local and central government.

Strategic vision

8.5. These flexible voting pilots form part of the government’s broader commitment to a transparent, secure, and inclusive democracy. As expectations of public services evolve, it is essential that electoral processes remain relevant, accessible, and trusted. Through these pilots, we aim to:

explore how voting can be made more convenient and inclusive

identify and address barriers to participation, particularly for underrepresented groups

test the operational and technological feasibility of new delivery models

ensure that any changes uphold the integrity and transparency of the electoral process

8.6. Importantly, these pilots represent the first step in a longer-term strategy to modernise the voting experience. The insights gained will inform future phases of reform, helping to shape a roadmap for wider implementation of successful models. This phased approach ensures that changes are supported by evidence, responsive to local needs, and capable of delivering a more inclusive and future-ready democratic process.

8.7. By working in partnership with local authorities, the government aims to build a stronger evidence base for future reforms and ensure that any changes to the voting process are grounded in real-world experience and robust evaluation.

9. FAQs

What are the flexible voting pilots aiming to achieve?

The pilots aim to test flexible voting methods that improve convenience, accessibility, and resilience in electoral delivery. They are designed to explore how innovations like early voting, and voting hubs can better meet the needs of today’s electorate while maintaining the integrity of the democratic process.

Can my authority propose a pilot model not listed in the prospectus?

Yes. While we have outlined two core options, local authorities may propose alternative models that respond to local needs. Any such proposals must be supported by a clear rationale and must not include online voting or electronic voting machines in polling stations.

Will funding be provided for pilot delivery?

Yes. MHCLG will provide funding via grants to cover the additional costs of piloting. Where changes result in savings, these should be used to offset costs to ensure value for money.

What support will be available to pilot authorities?

MHCLG, supported by the Electoral Commission and Association of Electoral Administrators, will work closely with selected authorities throughout the planning and delivery phases. We will share learning from previous pilots, provide guidance on statutory processes, and support engagement with suppliers and stakeholders.

How will supplier delivery be managed for the pilots?

Local authorities participating in the pilots will retain full responsibility for managing supplier relationships. This includes establishing and managing contractual arrangements, overseeing supplier activity, and ensuring that services are delivered in line with the pilot objectives. While MHCLG may engage with suppliers to support overall delivery, local authorities will remain responsible for effective governance, clear communication, and robust oversight of any third-party involvement.

Authorities should also consider supplier readiness and contingency planning as part of their delivery approach. We encourage local authorities to engage with suppliers during the application process to help demonstrate feasibility and deliverability of their proposed pilot. Authorities are responsible for ensuring that any supplier arrangements deliver value for money for the taxpayer and are supported by appropriate procurement, cost-control and contract-management arrangements. Early engagement with local authority procurement teams is encouraged.

Does my authority need prior experience using technology to manage polling station registers to take part in a pilot?

No. We are happy to work with local authorities regardless of their previous experience with technology in polling stations. Whether you have used electronic registers before or are exploring them for the first time, we will provide support to help you develop a suitable pilot model. The aim is to test what works in different contexts, so a mix of experience levels is welcome.

However, it is important to note that local authorities will be responsible for managing any suppliers involved in delivering technical solutions. This includes holding contractual arrangements, overseeing delivery, and ensuring that services meet the pilot’s objectives and standards.

Can authorities undergoing Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) take part in the pilots?

We recognise that some authorities may be undergoing or preparing for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR). Unfortunately, we are unable to accept applications from local authorities undergoing LGR.

Is it possible to run pilots at by-elections?

Under current legislation, a local authority must apply to pilot in relation to a specific election. Because by-elections are typically called at short notice, there is unlikely to be sufficient time to complete the formal application process and implement the necessary changes for a pilot scheme. As a result, pilots are only expected to take place at scheduled elections where planning and legislative requirements can be met.
